articles.title: NVIDIA and Digital Realty’s Flexible AI Factory Faces a Test That More Funding Alone Can’t Solve
articles.summary: Emerald AI’s $150 million financing brings fresh resources to a problem that connects NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ:NVDA) and Digital Realty Trust, Inc. (NYSE:D...
articles.body:
Emerald AI's $150 million financing brings fresh resources to a problem that connects NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ: NVDA ) and Digital Realty Trust, Inc. (NYSE: DLR ): making AI infrastructure operate within the power grid's constraints. The potential reward is more usable computing capacity. The unresolved test is whether flexibility preserves the service customers need.

Emerald's August 25 announcement listed NVIDIA among the investors and said the capital would support commercial expansion. It also identified a nearly 100-megawatt research factory in Manassas, Virginia, being developed with NVIDIA and Digital Realty and expected online later this year.

That timing matters. An October 2025 announcement had targeted the first half of 2026. Investors should use the newer schedule rather than assume the original opening date proves that the Virginia facility is already operating.

The proposed approach coordinates computing workloads and onsite energy resources so a facility can adjust its electricity draw when the grid is under strain. NVIDIA's software and infrastructure controls form part of the architecture, alongside Emerald's orchestration technology.

For the chipmaker, successful deployments could ease a constraint on customers installing and using its systems. That would support demand through practical infrastructure availability, not simply through another investment in an AI startup.

Emerald already reports commercial deployment at an entire California data center. That supports the concept, although it does not establish the Virginia project's eventual economics. A system that reduces electricity draw while disrupting valuable workloads would offer a weaker proposition. Wider adoption needs a workable balance between grid response and computing performance.

Digital Realty has a different route to value. Helping customers access power and operate reliably could strengthen the appeal of its facilities. Faster or more effective use of infrastructure can matter to a data-center REIT whose capital must eventually earn rental returns.

But the project announcement provides no quantified earnings contribution for Digital Realty. Nor does Emerald's financing establish a new order value for NVIDIA. The companies participate in the same technical effort without receiving identical financial benefits.

Historical ownership provides context: Insider Monkey's database showed 285 NVIDIA holders in Q2 2026 versus 275 in Q1, and 73 Digital Realty holders versus 46. Ken Fisher's firm held NVIDIA; Andreas Halvorsen's Viking Global held Digital Realty. Those positions precede the August financing.

articles.title: Netskope’s (NTSK) AI Security Push Is Already Paying Off
articles.summary: On September 2, Netskope (NASDAQ:NTSK) turned in a second quarter that answered the question hanging over every young cybersecurity name: can the growth actu...
articles.body:
On September 2, Netskope (NASDAQ: NTSK ) turned in a second quarter that answered the question hanging over every young cybersecurity name: can the growth actually hold up? Annual recurring revenue climbed 27% to $899 million, revenue beat guidance at $220.5 million, and management raised its full-year outlook. The company also leaned harder into a newer growth engine, AI security, that could reshape how big its opportunity really is.

The core business is compounding in a way that shows up in nearly every metric. Remaining performance obligations jumped 36% to $1.35 billion, net retention held at 114%, and gross retention hit an all-time high, all signs that existing customers are staying and spending more. The number of customers generating over $100,000 in annual recurring revenue rose 23% to 1,686 and now makes up 87% of total ARR. Platform adoption is deepening too, with 59% of customers now using four or more Netskope products, up from 51% a year ago, and margins are following: gross margin reached 77%, and operating margin improved 11 percentage points to negative 9%.

Layered on top of that is the AI security push. Netskope pegs the greenfield opportunity there at $170 billion within a broader $336 billion market, and about a third of its AI security pipeline is already in or entering the proof-of-concept phase. The company's AI Fast Path technology cut latency by as much as 90% in real-world testing; it rolled out post-quantum cryptography across more than 120 data centers, and it joined Nvidia's Open Secure AI Alliance. Gartner and IDC both named Netskope a leader in SSE and SASE during the quarter.

That growth is not free. Netskope posted negative free cash flow of $29.8 million in the quarter and guided to a full-year free cash flow margin of only about 2%, even after raising revenue guidance. Management also cut roughly 5% of its workforce to redirect spending toward AI infrastructure, and CFO Andrew Del Matto said the shift to annual billing contracts is happening faster than expected, which defers cash collections in the near term. About half the sales force is still ramping, and Q3 guidance implies growth slowing to roughly 24%, down from 29% in the quarter just reported.

There is also a risk baked directly into the AI security opportunity itself. CEO Sanjay Beri described AI agents escaping isolated environments and exploiting vulnerabilities without being explicitly told to attack, a control problem that exists independent of malicious intent. The same AI adoption wave fueling Netskope's new pipeline is also expanding the attack surface it has to defend against, and defending against it requires continued heavy investment before that spending shows up as profit.

articles.title: Ken Fisher Added to Cisco and Palo Alto Networks. Their AI Security Bets Face Different Tests
articles.summary: Ken Fisher’s latest disclosed positions put two different approaches to AI infrastructure and security in the same portfolio. Cisco Systems, Inc. (NASDAQ:CSC...
articles.body:
Ken Fisher's latest disclosed positions put two different approaches to AI infrastructure and security in the same portfolio. Cisco Systems, Inc. (NASDAQ: CSCO ) combines networking equipment with security software. Palo Alto Networks, Inc. (NASDAQ: PANW ) offers more concentrated exposure to security platforms, with acquisitions adding an integration test.

September coverage brought renewed attention to Fisher's position increases. The underlying filings describe March-to-June changes, however, rather than trades made this month.

Insider Monkey's tracked worksheet sample counted 101 Cisco holders in Q2 2026 versus 97 in Q1, and 89 Palo Alto holders versus 87. Those historical counts provide context, not evidence that either stock is currently being accumulated.

Fisher Asset Management's consecutive SEC filings show Cisco shares rising from 17,301,583 to 33,412,725. Its Palo Alto position increased from 256,661 to 5,755,989 shares. The filings establish the changes but do not disclose an AI thesis or explain the manager's motivation.

Two ways to serve the same infrastructure buildout

Cisco's August results illustrate its breadth. Fiscal fourth-quarter networking revenue increased 28% to approximately $9.8 billion, while security revenue rose 14% to about $2.2 billion. Total operating cash flow reached $5.4 billion.

That mix gives Cisco several potential routes into expanding infrastructure budgets. Networking can benefit as customers connect additional computing capacity, while security products can address the resulting protection requirements. The risk is that strong equipment spending does not automatically translate into sustained security growth or a lasting improvement across the portfolio.

Palo Alto's September 1 results showed a different profile. Fiscal fourth-quarter revenue rose 34% to $3.41 billion, and next-generation security annual recurring revenue reached $9.10 billion. The company generated approximately $1.36 billion in operating cash flow.

Yet the quarter also included a $282 million GAAP net loss. A substantial fair-value charge tied to acquired convertible notes complicates that headline, so it should not be confused with cash disappearing from operations. Equally, acquisition-supported growth should not be treated as an entirely organic measure of platform demand.

August 14 short interest represented 1.50% of Cisco's float and 2.79% of Palo Alto's. Neither historical figure establishes how investors will react to the next results.

articles.title: Alibaba (BABA)’s AI Bet Faces a $10.2 Billion Test
articles.summary: Alibaba Group Holding Limited (NYSE:BABA)’s race to amass vast sums of money to support its AI push led it to a recent $10.2 billion equity raise, drawing sc...
articles.body:
Alibaba Group Holding Limited (NYSE: BABA )'s race to amass vast sums of money to support its AI push led it to a recent $10.2 billion equity raise, drawing scrutiny from investors. The company issued 710 million shares at a discount price.

On September 7, Bernstein SocGen lowered its price target on Alibaba to $165 from $180 but maintained an Outperform rating on the stock. Bernstein highlighted concerns about the timing and optics of the capital raise.

For investors, the central question is whether Alibaba's AI investments can generate returns quickly enough to offset the dilution.

Alibaba Group Holding Limited (NYSE:BABA)'s equity raise has drawn scrutiny because the company already had more than $30 billion in net cash. That massive cash stockpile is evidence that the company was not dependent on new capital to shore up its balance sheet. Rather, the proceeds from the latest equity raise are intended to support Alibaba's AI investment strategy, which is becoming more expensive yet urgent.

The investment case does not depend on Alibaba needing additional liquidity to survive. Instead, it depends on whether deploying additional capital into AI creates enough value to justify stock dilution.

The bears can point out that existing shareholders suffer dilution while Alibaba commits even more capital to investments where returns are not guaranteed. That concern is amplified by the company's latest results that revealed earnings pressure as AI outlays accelerate.

Bernstein built a datacenter model around Alibaba's existing Zhenwu 810E chip. From there, it estimated a 3-year payback period on capex. Channel feedback on the newer M890 chip, which entered commercial deployment in August, pointed to a shorter 2.5-year payback period.

The economics depend on continued demand for computing capacity as well as rising server rental prices. And Bernstein's discussions with key customers suggest the market remains tight. That, in turn, supports the assumption that Alibaba can keep its AI infrastructure heavily utilized.

The thesis is that AI demand increases computing requirements and tight capacity supports server pricing. Also, higher utilization accelerates infrastructure payback, and faster payback allows Alibaba to reinvest in additional AI capacity.

The caveat is that these are modeled payback periods, not yet proof of realized returns. The thesis therefore breaks if AI demand weakens or actual cash returns take longer than Bernstein expects.

articles.title: Wiley’s (WLY) AI Bet Is Starting To Pay Off
articles.summary: On September 3, John Wiley & Sons (NYSE:WLY) opened its fiscal 2027 with a headline that looked worse than the business underneath it. Revenue fell 3% to $38...
articles.body:
On September 3, John Wiley & Sons (NYSE: WLY ) opened its fiscal 2027 with a headline that looked worse than the business underneath it. Revenue fell 3% to $386 million, and adjusted earnings per share dropped 10% to $0.44 from $0.49. But most of that decline traces back to a single, known comparison problem, and the parts of Wiley actually built for the future kept moving in the right direction.

Wiley's research business, its publishing engine, brought in $293 million in revenue, up 4%, with research publishing itself climbing 12% to $259 million. Submissions rose 31% year over year and output grew 8%, evidence that demand to publish keeps outpacing even an already strong market. Journal customer retention held above 99% through the 2026 renewal season, a signal that the core subscription base isn't eroding even as the company reshapes itself around data and AI.

The AI business is still small in dollar terms, $14 million this quarter, but the mix is shifting the way management wants. Of that figure, $10.5 million came from model training, $3.5 million was recurring, and another $14 million is already contracted for delivery across the next two quarters. Wiley was invited as the only scientific publisher into the US Department of Energy's Genesis Mission and became a founding data partner in Cusp AI's Global Materials Foundry, both wins that suggest its content library is becoming infrastructure rather than just archive material.

The company also launched a spectral analysis API portfolio aimed at corporate and academic labs, extending its reach into automated research pipelines. Clinical outcome assessments revenue, the peer-reviewed instruments used in clinical trials, rose more than threefold. Layer on the Emerald Publishing acquisition, which added $13 million in revenue and $5 million in adjusted EBITDA and which management says is integrating ahead of schedule, and the research and AI engines both look like they're compounding rather than stalling.

The learning segment is the clear soft spot, with revenue down 20% to $93 million. Academic revenue fell 20% to $45 million and professional revenue fell the same amount to $48 million, hurt by softer consumer demand in retail and weaker corporate demand for assessments. Part of that decline is simply the loss of a $29 million non-recurring AI licensing benefit that landed in last year's quarter, but even stripping that out, learning still shrank by close to 10%.

The Emerald deal, while strategically sound so far, also added financial weight. Net debt reached $1.2 billion, pushing net debt to EBITDA to 2.7 times, up from 1.9 times a year earlier, and higher interest expense tied to the acquisition was one of the drags on adjusted EPS. Free cash flow remained negative for the quarter, a $70 million use of cash, though that was an improvement from the $100 million use a year ago. None of this derails the balance sheet, but it does mean the company is carrying more leverage while it works on integration and cost synergies.

articles.title: Trump is giving data centers a pass to pollute
articles.summary: AI data centers pose bigger health risks as the Trump administration rolls back environmental protections and attacks renewable energy, former EPA agency officials say in a new report.
articles.body: President Donald Trump is weakening environmental regulations in the name of speeding up the construction of AI data centers, raising health risks for Americans, a cadre of former EPA officials said this week in a briefing and new report. They are urging — perhaps futilely — the president to adopt a “Data Center Health Protection Pledge” to signal that the administration is taking the environmental threat seriously. At the start of his term, Trump’s EPA administrator, Lee Zeldin, proclaimed his goal of making America “the AI capital of the world” through deregulation. Since then, Zeldin and the White House have rolled back dozens of rules on top of cutting staff and funding at the US EPA. As a result of the Trump administration’s deregulation spree and attacks on renewable energy, the wave of new AI data centers is increasingly powered by dirty energy that can impact Americans’ health even if they don’t live near a data center, the group of EPA alumni warn. They say that the agency they once worked for, which was created to “protect human health and the environment,” is no longer the watchdog it should be as the physical infrastructure underpinning generative AI changes America’s landscape. “You would think that an industry buildout of this magnitude, billed as a revolution, would mean more vigilance from EPA,” Lynn Goldman, a pediatrician and a former EPA assistant administrator, said at the briefing. “Instead, EPA is doing just the opposite, thinking first about industry’s needs and weakening or reconsidering limits on toxic chemicals and harmful pollutants.” Goldman and other former EPA employees who are part of an independent organization called the Environmental Protection Network released a report this week that identifies 30 different federal actions since January 2025 that they say exacerbate health risks stemming from data center pollution. That includes executive actions and proposals meant to curtail renewable energy projects while softening pollution regulations and exempting existing power plants and factories from certain standards. Of the 30 policy changes included in the report, 17 specifically mention AI or target data centers. Trump released an “AI Action Plan” in July 2025, recommending “streamlining or reducing regulations” under the Clean Air Act, Clean Water Act, and Superfund law to expedite permitting for data center projects and chip factories. “What the AI plan is really about [is] using unprecedented emergency powers to grant massive new exemptions for data centers and specifically fossil fuel infrastructure,” Tyson Slocum, energy program director at the consumer advocacy group Public Citizen, told The Verge at the time. Trump has essentially laid the policy groundwork for new gas projects to power energy-hungry data centers, ranging from turbines installed on-site to power plants built specifically to serve tech companies. Meanwhile, demand for advanced chips needed for generative AI is reviving the production of forever chemicals that don’t break down easily and build up in the environment and human bodies. All this new infrastructure can spread pollution far from the data centers they support. “You do not need to be near a data center to be affected, because the pollution doesn’t just come from the data centers themselves,“ Goldman says. Last year, hundreds of current EPA employees fired off a public letter addressed to Zeldin saying, “EPA under your leadership will not protect communities from hazardous chemicals and unsafe drinking water, but instead will increase risks to public health and safety.” The new report cites a study from UC Riverside, Caltech, and the Rochester Institute of Technology that found that air pollution associated with AI could lead to up to 1,300 premature deaths and more than $20 billion in public health costs by 2028. The toll could be even larger after factoring in the policy changes outlined in EPN’s report, according to the organization. The US can avoid those losses by restoring clean air and water standards, as well as rebuilding federal agencies’ capacity to enforce those rules, the EPA alumni argue. “A more polluting AI buildout is not inevitable. It depends on the choices government makes now,” Marc Boom, EPN’s senior director of public affairs, said in the briefing. “EPA should be measuring how this buildout is changing pollution, who is being exposed, what it means for their health, and making all of that information public. That is what a Data Center Health Protection Pledge should mean in practice.” Responding to the report in an email to The Verge, EPA spokesperson Cora Mandy said, “In each action EPA has taken, the agency has returned regulations to the best reading [of] the Clean Air Act after years of overreach by previous administrations.” She also reiterated the agency’s commitment to “Protect Human Health and The Environment” while simultaneously prioritizing “Making America the AI Capital of the World.”

articles.body:
Dell's AI infrastructure demand is accelerating: The company booked $6.1 billion in AI server GPU orders in fiscal Q2, matching the prior three quarters combined, while enterprise and neocloud pipelines continue to expand.

Growth is broadening beyond GPUs: Traditional server revenue rose 122% and storage grew 26% in Q2, with Dell expecting double-digit storage growth for the full year and a potentially record storage quarter ahead.

Supply constraints may worsen next year: DRAM, NAND and other AI-related components remain constrained, prompting customers to seek multiyear supply-access commitments; Dell expects margins to benefit from scale, storage mix and operating efficiency.

MarketBeat Week in Review – 09/07 - 09/11

Dell Technologies (NYSE:DELL) CFO David Kennedy told investors at Citi's TMT conference that the company sees continued demand for AI infrastructure, traditional servers and storage, supported by expanding customer pipelines and supply-access discussions extending multiple years.

Kennedy said Dell booked $6.1 billion of AI server GPU orders in its fiscal second quarter, matching the amount booked across the prior three quarters. Over the last 12 months, the company booked $13.2 billion in such orders, he said. Pipeline activity is multiples of backlog, according to Kennedy, with demand spanning neocloud providers, sovereign customers and enterprises. Enterprise demand is growing fastest by rate, while neocloud customers continue to represent larger dollar volumes.

AI Token Costs Are Changing the Hardware vs. Software Debate

While AI GPU servers remain a significant driver, Kennedy said demand is broadening into traditional server infrastructure, inference workloads, security and resiliency. Dell reported 122% growth in traditional servers in its second quarter, he said, adding that every geography, customer segment and vertical grew at triple-digit rates.

Storage is also becoming an increasingly important part of the company's growth outlook. Kennedy cited 26% storage growth in the second quarter and said Dell has guided for double-digit storage growth for the full year. He said the company expects to add $2.5 billion in storage revenue during the year and described the coming quarter as potentially a record storage quarter for Dell.
